summary: Durango sits on both sides of Mexico's protective-law gradient. It passed Decreto 356, formally typifying transfeminicide in state law, part of the wave of state statutes (following Nayarit's March 2024 first-in-country definition) that recognise gender-motivated killing as an aggravated offence. Yet Human Rights Watch's March 2025 country review lists Durango among the six states that have reformed nothing to create a legal gender-recognition procedure - a mismatch between symbolic criminal law and the administrative vacuum that leaves identity documents permanently unfixable and is the most visitor-relevant legal fact in Mexico. As with the other state transfeminicide statutes, national reporting finds the laws advancing 'in law but not in sentences', so they mark official climate rather than enforcement.

Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024): documents how the absence of any legal gender-recognition procedure in Tabasco exposes trans people to police stops, denial of documents and institutional mistreatment - the country's clearest case of administrative erasure, cited to establish what a state without any procedure does to trans residents and visitors.

The Guardian global-development report (24 July 2024): Mexico City criminalised transfeminicide with sentences up to 70 years after the 2016 killing of trans sex worker Paola Buenrostro whose attacker was released despite footage and witnesses and remains at large; activists call the law a watershed in one of Latin America's deadliest countries for trans people, while the reporting notes convictions lag the statute - the benchmark for judging other states' transfeminicide laws.
